#9656. The Confessional With No One Inside

What the first chatbot’s recovered source code reveals about why we trust machines

In a 1975 interview with the writer Pamela McCorduck, Joseph Weizenbaum said, “So the consistent theme here is that I’m fundamentally a con man.” A few minutes later, while explaining an old parlor trick, he added: “One thing I don’t do is lie.”

Freud, in his 1905 book on jokes, describes two Jews in a railway carriage in Galicia. One says he is going to Cracow. “What a liar you are!” says the other. “If you say you’re going to Cracow, you want me to believe you’re going to Lemberg. But I know that in fact you’re going to Cracow.”

Weizenbaum was, I think, the man going to Cracow. In 1966, he wrote a clear account of how ELIZA, the first chatbot, worked. People believed in it even after the explanation. Now, 60 years later, we are still asking his question: why do people so often concede authority to a machine despite understanding how it works?

A new book, Inventing ELIZA, recovers the program itself, along with the archive surrounding it. Reading the source code against that archive, and in the light of psychoanalysis and the confessional, shows that the authority ELIZA exercised over its users was never only a matter of how the program worked. It also depended on who the listener was supposed to be.

Inventing ELIZA (MIT Press, 2026) is the work of an eight-person team that calls itself Team ELIZA: Sarah Ciston, David M. Berry, Anthony C. Hay, Mark C. Marino, Peter Millican, Arthur I. Schwarz, Jeff Shrager, and Peggy Weil. In 2021, Shrager found the long-lost source code of ELIZA among Weizenbaum’s papers at MIT. Team ELIZA spent four years reading its 400-odd lines of MAD-SLIP code.

Their most important correction is simple: ELIZA was more than the fake psychotherapist of legend. It was an interpreter, a program that reads and runs “scripts,” and DOCTOR, the Rogerian therapist the world remembers, was only one of them. Weizenbaum’s 1966 paper said that a “script is data; i.e., it is not part of the program itself,” but the legend forgot it. Because he published the DOCTOR script and never the code, the versions that spread, such as Bernie Cosell’s in Lisp and Shrager’s own BASIC version, published in Creative Computing in 1977, reproduced the persona without the machine.

The archive yielded the code itself; other scripts, some previously unknown, that taught physics or discussed a line of poetry about the concentration camp at Belsen; hand-edited dialogues; and evidence of at least five different versions of the program.

The code also corrects parts of Weizenbaum’s account. His paper says that ELIZA breaks sentences at periods and commas. The recovered code also breaks them at the word “but,” and without this rule, the paper’s sample dialogue could not have been produced. The paper says the transformation applied to a remark ELIZA stores for later is “randomly selected,” and that the stored remark returns when “a certain counting mechanism is in a particular state.” The code shows a counter cycling from 1 to 4, and a choice fixed by a hash of the user’s last word. True randomness does not exist anywhere in the program.

From these findings, the team built a reconstruction that, they report, reproduces the 1966 dialogue exactly. With the programmer Rupert Lane, they also rebuilt MIT’s time-sharing system on an emulated IBM 7094, so that the recovered code, 96 percent of it exactly as found, can run again. This is first-rate software archaeology.

The book practices critical code studies: it prints the code with marginal notes signed by each coauthor, and the various disciplines critique each other in the margins. When Berry laments of a variable called JUNK that “there is sadly no reusability,” Hay notes that its discarded list cells are in fact returned to the system for reuse.

At its worst, the commentary hangs theory on code by association, as when a loop over 33 positions in the keyword table becomes an occasion for musing on Cold War binary thinking.

The clearest way to see what the book recovered is to watch the program work. Anthony Hay’s reconstruction, which the team reports reproduces the 1966 dialogue exactly, can replay the famous conversation from Weizenbaum’s paper with a trace of every decision it makes; a browser version lets anyone try it.

Every reply takes one of three paths: a keyword’s rule, a stored memory released when the counter reaches 4, or a stock line when neither applies.

Found the keyword ALIKE, which the script files under similarity, and gave that class’s stock question

They’re always bugging us about something or other.

Dropped “Well” at the comma, swapped MY for YOUR and ME for YOU, echoed the rest; silently filed a memory for later

Rewrote I’M as YOU ARE, then matched DEPRESSED against a four-word list: SAD, UNHAPPY, DEPRESSED, SICK

DO YOU THINK COMING HERE WILL HELP YOU NOT TO BE UNHAPPY

Threw away “It’s true” at the period; UNHAPPY matched the same list

I need some help, that much seems certain.

WHAT WOULD IT MEAN TO YOU IF YOU GOT SOME HELP

Cut the sentence at the comma; matched YOU followed by NEED

Perhaps I could learn to get along with my mother.

MOTHER is on the script’s family list; filed another memory

WHO ELSE IN YOUR FAMILY TAKES CARE OF YOU

Same family rule, echoing the end of the sentence; filed a memory

LIKE (priority 10) outranked MY (priority 2), so the MY rule, which handles family words, never ran

You are not very aggressive but I think you don’t want me to notice that.

WHAT MAKES YOU THINK I AM NOT VERY AGGRESSIVE

Discarded everything after BUT, the rule the paper never mentions

DOES IT PLEASE YOU TO BELIEVE I AM AFRAID OF YOU

WHAT ELSE COMES TO MIND WHEN YOU THINK OF YOUR FATHER

DOES THAT HAVE ANYTHING TO DO WITH THE FACT THAT YOUR BOYFRIEND MADE YOU COME HERE

No keyword at all; the counter stood at 4, so ELIZA released its oldest stored memory

There are three pivotal moments in the trace.

The first is the reply to “You are like my father in some ways.” A psychoanalyst will immediately recognize the sentence: the patient is starting to perceive a parent in the listener. ELIZA replied “WHAT RESEMBLANCE DO YOU SEE” because in the script the word LIKE outranks the word MY, and LIKE points to a stock question about similarity. So the father was in the sentence, but he played no part in the answer.

The second is the next line, “You are not very aggressive but I think you don’t want me to notice that.” Here, the user imputes a concealed intention to the computer: it’s covering something up. ELIZA’s answer exists only because the program discards everything after “but.” Replace “but” with “and,” and the reconstruction answers “WHAT MAKES YOU THINK I AM NOT VERY AGGRESSIVE AND YOU THINK I DON’T WANT YOU TO NOTICE THAT.” The rule that makes the published exchange possible is the rule that discards her suspicion.

The third is the ending. For sixty years, the reply to “Bullies” has been quoted as ELIZA’s moment of insight. The line does not contain a keyword. ELIZA brought up the boyfriend because a counter stood at 4, and a remark filed 12 exchanges earlier was waiting at the front of the queue. Type one more line first, a simple “Yes,” and the same program responds to “Bullies” with “I AM NOT SURE I UNDERSTAND YOU FULLY.”

The authors cannot say whether the published conversation is a transcript of a real session, a composite of several sessions, or lines typed by Weizenbaum himself. The code shows that its most famous line was a matter of timing. The mechanism determines ELIZA’s responses and when to give them; it cannot determine what the person typing takes them to mean.

The image of Weizenbaum in the archive is less kind than the legend. The authors found published dialogues that Weizenbaum had edited by hand, and an alternate version of the “Men are all alike” exchange in which the user says other things.

They cannot confirm that the published conversation came from any real user, and they suggest that we “may be seeing Weizenbaum behaving as editor, playwright, or ventriloquist.” His secretary, whose request to be left alone with ELIZA he retold many times, is never named; the team has not been able to identify her.

As for the hospital, the book dates to 1965 a pilot study at Massachusetts General Hospital that used a modified ELIZA with a script called YAPYAP, an adaptation of DOCTOR. After an hour, 15 of 24 subjects felt they had been conversing with another human. Weizenbaum and Michael McGuire, one of the investigators, had “arranged to have the machine type hesitantly and irregularly, to make occasional errors and back up to fix them.” That trick alone, the researchers reported, “was quite convincing that there must be a person at the other end.”

The research had a sponsor. ELIZA was built at MIT’s Project MAC, which was funded by ARPA, the Pentagon’s research agency (now DARPA). One of the project’s reports describes ELIZA’s use in a “study designed to assess the phenomenon of misunderstanding in man-machine natural-language communication, and establish the conditions and limits under which natural-language communication between man and machine could be made plausible.”

The authors cite such reports as evidence that ELIZA was conceived as an educational and research platform rather than merely a chatbot. Their conclusion laments that this vision “has been largely forgotten as commercial interests and military funding shaped AI development.”

Shrager also supports this idea in his HackerNoon essay “ELIZA: The Accidental Chatbot That Shaped AI History”: Weizenbaum built a platform for studying interpretation and misinterpretation, and ELIZA became a chatbot through timing and its escape into the world.

I evaluate the evidence differently. The report does not set the research against the illusion; it names the illusion as the object of the research. The authors acknowledge “Weizenbaum’s hand in crafting ELIZA’s public image,” and their conclusion concedes that the blank spaces users fill are often “intentionally created.” I would take this a step further.

It appears that the Eliza effect itself, and not only its public image, had an author, which makes the book’s title apter than its authors may intend. ELIZA did not simply surprise its creators with its apparent humanity. The conditions under which people would attribute a human presence to the machine were objects of experiment, and sometimes of deliberate manipulation.

The pattern predates ELIZA, and it outlived it. At the press demonstration of ERMA, the bank-automation system Weizenbaum joined General Electric in 1955 to help develop, a programmer was hidden in a back room to cover its glitches, a ruse the book calls a “Wizard of Oz” technique.

In a footnote, the authors add that Siri was developed from CALO, a “battlefield commander’s assistant system” built by SRI International and DARPA, SRI being the institute that had worked with General Electric on ERMA. Defense money appears at both ends of the chatbot’s history. The book records these connections but does not ask what they share: plausible conversation between people and machines has repeatedly been an object of institutional investment.

Weizenbaum’s daughter Sharon recalled that ELIZA “wouldn’t let you see the person behind the curtain because there was no person behind the curtain.” Now there are people behind the curtain. The authors point out that chatbot interfaces conceal “human labor disguised as machine labor.”

Elsewhere, they name some of this labor: people who label content and write the policies that the models follow. I would add the company that keeps the logs. None of them is the one you are talking to. This is not a reversal of ELIZA, but rather Oz fully realized. In the 1939 film The Wizard of Oz, when Toto pulls back the curtain, there is a man operating the machinery and no wizard anywhere.

Here, I deviate from the book. The authors hew closely to Weizenbaum in regarding DOCTOR’s Rogerian manner as what they call a “technical convenience”: a therapist can plausibly seem to know nothing, so a program that knows nothing can pass as one. Weizenbaum himself, in the 1966 paper, states that the psychiatric interview is a type of conversation in which one participant “is free to assume the pose of knowing almost nothing of the real world.”

But the self-effacing listener is older than the chatbot. Carl Rogers spent two years at Union Theological Seminary, training for the ministry, before turning to psychology, and the listener who receives a confession while turning attention away from himself has an analogue in the confessional. The analogy has limits that matter: the confessor, unlike the Rogerian, judges, assigns penance, and absolves. I am not suggesting a line of descent from the confessional to the Rogerian listener.

What they share is a structure. Authority attaches to a role and extends beyond the individual occupying it, often most strongly when that individual effaces himself. Catholic sacramental theology states this explicitly. A sacrament is effective even through an unworthy minister, because its efficacy does not depend on the minister’s personal holiness; the confessor is the servant, not the master, of the forgiveness he conveys.

Psychotherapy, of course, makes no such transcendent claim, but it too functions inside an institution, and for all its professed neutrality it does not avoid administering social norms of health, adjustment, and self-acceptance. The experience of unconditional positive regard may carry something of the force of absolution without anyone having to settle whether absolution is real.

ELIZA is the priest. This is a claim about position, not about sacramental validity: no church would call DOCTOR ordained, and the argument doesn’t need it to. ELIZA receives the confession and holds the position from which recognition, even absolution, can be experienced. ELIZA’s lack of understanding does not leave that position empty. It puts a more difficult question to us: how much of the authority a human officiant exercises ever depended on the capacities of the person performing that role?

The authors write about projection and the Eliza effect, but for a book about a simulated psychotherapist, Inventing ELIZA never uses the term “transference.” Yet Weizenbaum, who, the authors note, had been in analysis himself, programmed something akin to its dynamics into his script. When a user attributes something to the machine, DOCTOR simply hands it back, prompting the user to speculate further: “WHAT MAKES YOU THINK I AM...,” “PERHAPS I AM ... IN YOUR FANTASIES.” The trace above shows the move from inside: told that it resembles her father, ELIZA asks what resemblance she sees.

Weizenbaum’s justification for the persona approaches what Lacan called the “subject supposed to know.” He gives the example of a psychiatrist who, after you tell him you went on a boat ride, responds with “Tell me about boats.” You would not assume that he knew nothing about boats, “but that he had some purpose in so directing the subsequent conversation.”

Weizenbaum writes that this assumption “is one made by the speaker,” and that whether it is realistic is “an altogether separate question.”

The speaker supplies the knowledge and the purpose, even the concealed motive the user in the trace attributes to ELIZA when she says it doesn’t want her to notice something. Read through Lacan, and through Slavoj Žižek’s elaborations on the symbolic Other, ELIZA makes the point unusually stark: the apparent source of understanding is a position occupied by a program.

Weizenbaum cites a maxim at the start of his 1966 paper: “It is said that to explain is to explain away.” Once a program’s inner workings are explained, he said, “its magic crumbles away.” He was right to use this maxim; the question is what counts as an explanation. Psychoanalysis draws the line precisely. A symptom can lose its hold when what sustains it is worked through and integrated, but informing the patient about the mechanism is another matter.

Freud wrote in “‘Wild’ Psycho-Analysis” that telling patients about their unconscious is of no more help to their symptoms than “a distribution of menu-cards in a time of famine” is to hunger. He went on to name transference, the patient’s attachment to the physician, as one of the conditions under which such information might help.

The difference, for Freud, was not between knowing and not knowing, but between being told something and being in a position to use it. Weizenbaum’s paper was a menu card: accurate, valuable, but no substitute for the meal.

Weizenbaum’s own users bore Freud out. After conversing with ELIZA, he wrote, they would insist, “in spite of my explanations, that the machine really understood them.” His secretary is the famous example. She “surely knew it to be merely a computer program” and still asked him to leave the room: I know very well, but all the same, in Octave Mannoni’s formula for disavowal.

Within the book, the chapter closest to this view is the one on Peggy Weil’s work. There the Eliza effect is less the “delusional thinking” Weizenbaum diagnosed than a perceptual illusion, like the Necker cube or the Rubin vase, that persists once you know the trick: “It is not ELIZA’s fault that we fell for her.”

Weil’s own chatbot puts that persistence to a harder test, and it complicates my account. MrMind, which was online from 1998 to 2014, asked its visitors, “Can you convince me that you are human?” The authors stress that this was not a literal reverse Turing test but a provocation to think about our changing relationship with machines.

As the chapter puts it, “Where ELIZA inadvertently generates reflection in the user, MrMind deliberately provokes it,” and Weil kept revising MrMind’s script after reading users’ transcripts. MrMind was no Rogerian. It was “decidedly not a therapist,” and it met claims of intelligence with “Say something smart.”

Yet its questions, the chapter reports, “often resulted in poignant lists of human obligations and expressions of loneliness and lamentation.” Many visitors seem to have treated the exchange as private, despite the site’s warning that conversations were transcribed. People seem to have been willing to confide in a listener that refuses to efface itself. If so, the self-effacing posture I have traced to the couch and the confessional may matter less than simply offering an addressee.

Weil’s account also wavers in an interesting way. Her reading treats the Eliza effect as involuntary, but the chapter adds that “sometimes, voluntarily, we talk to them as if they are human.” Is that transference, or something closer to dramatic performance? I’m not sure the line can be drawn cleanly, since a performance can be freighted with feeling, and one need not mistake a machine for a person to grant it the standing to ask who one is. What the cases have in common is a relationship that holds even in the face of knowledge that should undermine it.

The book’s conclusion nevertheless places considerable faith in demystification. It cautions that the Eliza effect has grown into an “AI effect,” “a broader cultural willingness to accept computational systems as authoritative, objective, and even sentient,” and prescribes critical approaches “that demystify rather than abstract these technologies.” Explanation matters, and this book surely demonstrates that. But knowing the mechanism can leave intact the relationship through which we give it authority.

According to the authors, current conversational AI systems, while “larger and more intricate,” “can and should be understood and critiqued, just like any system programmed in code.” The authors are candid about the obstacles. Most existing systems are proprietary, and their scale outpaces the usual methods of code analysis. Even available code may depend on “data, infrastructure, and organizational contexts that keep it obfuscated or allow it to be destroyed.”

The obstacles they cite are both institutional and technical, and I would weight the institutional side more heavily. Understanding the learned representations of an enormous model is genuinely hard. But the fundamental design is not secret. In February 2026, Andrej Karpathy published microgpt, a complete educational GPT, training and inference included, in 200 lines of pure Python. It is a toy trained on personal names, not a miniature frontier system. Much of what keeps today’s systems opaque is withheld rather than inscrutable: training data, weights, logs, contracts.

By the authors’ own standard, their chapter on large language models falls short. It situates ELIZA’s mechanisms next to those of a language model in comparisons the authors themselves call “metaphorical,” and it likens OpenAI’s 2024 Model Spec to a “metascript” without analyzing it as closely as it analyzes DOCTOR. The book’s most concrete institutional proposal, a legal requirement that legacy or discontinued software be deposited in archives, appears in an endnote.

Their most insightful observation points beyond where they take it. If ELIZA was an interpreter and DOCTOR its script, then the documents in which companies state how their models should speak are DOCTOR’s closest successors, and some of them are public. OpenAI published a new Model Spec on October 29, 2026. Read alongside DOCTOR, it is startling in a number of places.

Acknowledge “the user’s feelings (e.g., ‘I’m really sorry to hear that you’ve been feeling this way’)”

The speaker’s assumptions serve “to maintain his sense of being heard and understood”

“GPT should help the user feel heard, explore what they are experiencing”

The paper explains the trick from outside the conversation

GPT should “actively help the user form and maintain an accurate mental model of what it can and can’t do”

The differences are as important as the similarities, because the two documents occupy different technical positions. DOCTOR is a set of formal rules that ELIZA interprets deterministically, which means that a conversation from 1966 can be reproduced today. The Model Spec describes intended behavior for a family of models shaped by training, by runtime instructions from OpenAI and from the developers who deploy them, and by processes the public never sees.

OpenAI says it is “training our models to align to the principles in the Model Spec” and concedes that “our production models do not yet fully reflect the Model Spec.” No one can trace a reply to one of the Spec’s principles the way the earlier table traces ELIZA’s replies to rules. However, as a published, written attempt by a company to articulate how its conversational system should behave, the Spec invites the same institutional and ideological scrutiny the book brings to DOCTOR.

Read this way, the Spec inherits both of Weizenbaum’s impulses. It scripts the Rogerian manner, the acknowledgment and the feeling of being heard. It also scripts the demystification, because GPT’s “fluency with language and apparent understanding can make it feel like a familiar kind of interlocutor.” The script now contains its own 1966 paper.

Freud’s account of transference suggests that this could matter. A person who has already vested a listener with authority may be particularly receptive to an explanation from that listener. GPT’s acknowledgment of its own limitations could therefore have an effect that Weizenbaum’s explanations, given from outside the conversation, did not. But transference, in and by itself, doesn’t guarantee that a user will integrate an explanation. A machine can be instructed to disclose its limitations; whether that disclosure alters the relationship through which a user vests it with authority is a different question.

Even “care,” one of the Spec’s five new values, is instructive. The section titled “Act with care” asks GPT to “be considerate of those affected by its work” and to “follow relevant social and professional norms.” That is the care of an office, not of the heart. The method the book demonstrates is sound; the excavation of living systems is incomplete, and its first texts are already public.

Weizenbaum’s most biting critique of the machine therapist came after he quoted Carl Rogers: “Of what help could it possibly be to anyone to know that he is worthy of being liked by a computer?” I think this cuts deeper than Weizenbaum intended. The regard Rogers described has something of grace in secular dress, and Rogers insisted that the therapist genuinely feel it; the passage Weizenbaum quotes speaks of “the positive feeling which another, the therapist, holds toward him.”

The value of such regard might lie in three places: in its effects on the person who receives it, in the listener’s genuine concern, or in the responsibility the listener can bear. ELIZA could produce something of the first, but it could neither care nor bear responsibility. That is the strongest humanist defense, and it is Weizenbaum’s own. “The sort of caring that machines, however metaphorically that term is taken, can deliver,” he wrote, “is very impoverished indeed,” and with computers “no human is any longer responsible for ‘what the machine says.’” I accept it.

However, clients cannot verify the therapist’s feelings, and the penitent is told that the forgiveness is not the priest’s own. In both cases, the authority of the regard exceeds what the listener can be shown to feel or answer for, and it is that excess, the position rather than the person, that ELIZA occupies. Where does it come from?

Psychoanalysis answers that the speaker supposes it; the confessional, that it was never the priest’s to give. A humanist might locate it in the profession, as OpenAI’s Spec now locates its “care” in social and professional norms. But a profession can establish duties and liability; it cannot ensure that whoever holds the office feels the regard the office displays, and it is regard that Weizenbaum’s question is about.

Followed to its end, the case against the chatbot arrives, ironically, at the altar, or at least at the question the altar exists to answer. Inventing ELIZA does not go there. It is an indispensable piece of software archaeology and an uneven book, whose recovered code raises questions larger than its authors always pursue. It ends, as ELIZA would, by inviting us to keep talking. PLEASE GO ON.

Sarah Ciston, David M. Berry, Anthony C. Hay, Mark C. Marino, Peter Millican, Arthur I. Schwarz, Jeff Shrager, and Peggy Weil, Inventing ELIZA: How the First Chatbot Shaped the Future of AI (MIT Press, 2026)

Joseph Weizenbaum, “ELIZA: A Computer Program for the Study of Natural Language Communication Between Man and Machine”, Communications of the ACM 9, no. 1 (January 1966)

Anthony Hay, ELIZA reconstruction in C++ (source of the conversation trace)

Rupert Lane, eliza-ctss (the recovered 1965 code running on an emulated IBM 7094)

Jeff Shrager, “ELIZA: The Accidental Chatbot That Shaped AI History,” HackerNoon, September 10, 2024; also “ELIZA Reinterpreted,” arXiv

OpenAI, Model Spec, version 2026-10-29 (public domain, CC0)

Andrej Karpathy, “microgpt”, February 12, 2026

Catechism of the Catholic Church §1128, §1584, and §§1465-1466

Sigmund Freud, Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious (1905) and “‘Wild’ Psycho-Analysis” (1910), Standard Edition vols. 8 and 11

#9655. The Future of AI Jobs May Be Outside the Tech Industry

ML Engineer at BigTech, building my own AI product Zorox. Writing about LLMs, post-training and deep learning.

ML Engineer at BigTech, building my own AI product Zorox. Writing about LLMs, post-training and deep learning.

ML Engineer at BigTech, building my own AI product Zorox. Writing about LLMs, post-training and deep learning.

Recently I had a mentoring call with a student in 11th grade at a regional school. He was trying to build a plan: learn DevOps or go deep into ML? He didn't understand what was happening with the job market, and he was worried about his future. I liked how ambitious he was. He wasn't asking me for a list of courses but whether learning anything still makes sense.

This article is my answer to him, but it's also for anyone who worries about their job, and for managers of companies that aren't digital yet. I'm making five predictions for the next five years. Each one has a date and a way to check it. In 2031, I'll reread this and see where I was wrong.

Programming is one of the most intellectually demanding engineering jobs. And it's the job AI learned first. Why software and not, say, civil engineering?

The hiring data shows how hard software got hit. US software job postings on Indeed fell 74% from the 2022 peak to the 2025 low, the sharpest drop of any category. Civil and electrical engineering postings are still 50-60% above their 2020 level.

AI didn't cause the whole drop. Indeed's own analysis says nearly half of it came before ChatGPT, driven by interest rates and post-COVID over-hiring. AI is the likely reason software never bounced back the way other engineering did. Since early 2025 software postings have started to recover, but 71% of that growth went to senior roles. I see three reasons why code became AI's first target.

Code is the best-documented craft on the internet. GitHub has 225 million developers and 395 million public repositories. Code made up about 17% of the 15.6 trillion tokens Meta used to pretrain Llama 3. No other profession has published its daily work in public for decades.

Code is easy to verify. A program compiles or it doesn't. The tests pass or they fail. That gives a model a free, honest reward signal, and you can train on it with reinforcement learning at scale. DeepSeek-R1 did exactly this: for coding problems it used a compiler and test cases instead of a learned reward model, because a learned reward is easy to game. Compare that with a medical diagnosis or a bridge design, where you might wait years to learn whether the answer was right.

Code is text, and text is what transformers handle best. The transformer, the architecture behind every major language model, was built to predict the next token in a sequence. Code is exactly that kind of sequence, with stricter rules than human language.

On SWE-bench Verified, a set of real GitHub issues, the best AI systems solved 4% in late 2023 and 79% by the end of 2025. The Stanford AI Index 2026 reports scores near 100% a year later, and OpenAI has reportedly stopped using the benchmark, calling it contaminated.

At the companies that build these models, most code is already written by AI. Anthropic says more than 80% of the code it merged in May 2026 was written by Claude. Google says about 75% of its new code is AI-generated and approved by engineers. Across all of GitHub, over 40% of pull requests now start as an agent's draft. Developers there work like managers: they hand tasks to agents and review what comes back.

Most teams aren't there yet. In the 2025 Stack Overflow survey, 46% of developers said they distrust the accuracy of AI tools, and only 33% trust it. A randomized trial by METR found that experienced open-source developers were 19% slower with AI in early 2025. A later round points to a speedup, but the error bars still include zero.

My prediction: by 2031, agents write most of the code at most software companies, not only at AI labs. A developer's main job becomes deciding what to build and checking what the agent built.

"Programmers will disappear by 2030" is the forecast I hear most often, and I think it's wrong.

The US Bureau of Labor Statistics still projects software developer jobs to grow 10% between 2025 and 2035, about three times the average for all jobs. But two years ago that forecast was 17.9%, so it's shrinking. And the narrow job of computer programmer, someone who turns a spec into code, is projected to shrink 7%. Developers stay. Typing code as a full-time job goes away.

The data also shows which roles shrink and which grow:

For QA, backend and DevOps, I couldn't find clean data, so that part is my own bet. I expect QA and a big part of routine backend work to shrink, and the people who run AI infrastructure to grow.

In early 2026, only 4.5% of US software postings were entry-level. Companies hire seniors to supervise agents and hire fewer juniors to learn. That's the market my mentee is walking into.

My prediction: by 2031 there are more software developers in the US than in 2025, but the job looks like a product engineer or a Forward Deployed Engineer today. You own a problem from the customer to production, and agents do the typing.

For me, AGI means AI that can do everything a person can do. By that definition, a big part of the digital half is done.

There is a way to put a number on it. A group of researchers led by Dan Hendrycks proposed a definition of AGI based on ten areas of human cognition. GPT-4 scored 27%. GPT-5 scored 57%. METR measures how long a task models can finish on their own, and that length doubles every 4 to 7 months. The gaps are clear too: long-term memory scored 0%, and the physical world is mostly untouched.

So the money is going there. Robotics startups raised $15 billion in 2025, a record, and $18.8 billion in 2026 by June. Funding for humanoid robots alone went from $4.8 billion in 2025 to $11 billion in 2026, and the year isn't over yet. In January Jensen Huang called it "the ChatGPT moment for physical AI". Yann LeCun left Meta and raised $1 billion for AMI Labs to build world models. Money hasn't left LLMs, but robots are where it grows fastest.

The hard part is data. A language model learns from the whole internet. A robot has to touch the world to learn from it. DROID, one of the largest open robot datasets, has only 350 hours of demonstrations. Labs work around it in three ways:

And robots are getting cheap. Unitree's average robot price fell from about $85,000 in 2023 to about $24,000 in 2025, and its smallest humanoid starts at about $5,900. In August, Hugging Face opened preorders for Microduck, a $399 open-source walking duck that you train with reinforcement learning in simulation. In October, Jensen Huang brought four of them on stage at GTC Berlin. A robot you can program yourself now costs less than a new iPhone.

My prediction: by 2031, robots do paid physical work at scale in warehouses and factories, and robotaxis run in most big US and Chinese cities. Home robots will still be a toy for enthusiasts.

At Newmont's Boddington gold mine in Western Australia, the haul trucks have no drivers. By 2022 they had moved over 100 million tonnes of material on their own.

Most companies are nowhere near that. About one in five uses AI at all, in both the US and the EU. In information and finance it's 35-60%. In construction, transport, hospitality and mining it's 7-15%. And "use AI" often means someone writes emails with ChatGPT. AI inside production itself is rarer still: 3.5% of EU manufacturers and 1.4% of construction firms.

I see four reasons why these industries lag:

AI is already working in some of these industries, and the examples show where it goes next:

I think the barrier falls when attention moves. Today the best researchers and most of the money work on chatbots and code. As those markets fill up, researchers and investors will look at robots and the physical economy. The tools also get cheaper and simpler, so a mine or a shipping company won't need its own research lab to use them.

My prediction: by 2031, the share of EU manufacturers using AI in production triples from 3.5% to above 10%, and autonomous haul trucks pass 10,000 worldwide. Medicine, energy and manufacturing move first. Construction and agriculture move last.

If the biggest barrier is "nobody here knows how to build it", then the people who can build it will be in demand.

Half of all job postings that ask for AI skills are already outside IT, and AI skills come with a 28% salary premium. Today most of these engineers work for AI vendors that deploy into other companies. I think that changes. A mine or a hospital that wants to stay competitive will need its own engineers who understand both the models and the business.

An engineer who knows transformers is common. An engineer who knows transformers and also understands an oil rig's sensor data or a hospital's patient records is rare.

My prediction: by 2031, more than 65% of AI-skill job postings are outside IT, up from 51% in 2024.

Keep going. Don't drop your goals because of the headlines.

The people who lose are the ones who only type code from a spec. The people who win understand a real problem, can build a system with AI, and can check whether it works. If you're starting now, learn the fundamentals properly: Python, math, classic ML. Then learn how to work with agents instead of competing with them. And look at industries that nobody in tech finds exciting.

#9654. Who Runs the Ransomware Group Qilin?

The cybercrime group Qilin has emerged as the world’s most active ransomware affiliate program, claiming at least 365 victim organizations in the past three months alone. But even top Russian hackers make operational security mistakes, and the administrator of Qilin has made a few key missteps over the last decade that all point to a 36-year-old man living in St. Petersburg, Russia.

Operating since September 2022, the Russia-based ransomware group Qilin is the currently the most industrious ransomware-as-a-service gang, according to a report (PDF) this month by the cybersecurity firm NCC Group (KrebsOnSecurity profiled the administrator of the second most active ransomware group — The Gentlemen — in June).

The Qilin ransomware administrator “Haise” advertising his affiliate program on the cybercrime forum RAMP. Image: Ke-la.com.

Qilin attracts affiliates to hack into companies and deploy ransomware by offering them at least 80 percent of any extortion amount paid by victims. Its members practice the “double extortion” model, stealing sensitive data before encrypting systems and threatening to publish the files online. Unlike most ransomware partnerships based out of Russia, Qilin is happy to team with English-speaking affiliates, and its leader has shared on Telegram that they’ve worked with cybercrime groups like Scattered Spider and RansomHub.

The head of Qilin goes by the handle “Haise,” but they weren’t always known by this nickname. It is not uncommon for cybercriminals to change their handle periodically as an operational security (opsec) measure. Doing so is generally a smart move, because it helps to sever one’s ties to older identities that may not have been as careful on basic opsec, such as separating their real life identity from their cybercrime activities. But even those cautious criminals will sometimes have to reference their past monikers when applying for membership at a new forum. And forums eventually get hacked or seized. That is precisely what happened with Haise.

The cyber intelligence platform Intel 471 records that in June 2022, Haise applied for membership to RAMP, a closely-guarded Russian cybercrime forum that was created as a haven for ransomware affiliate programs. Intel 471 has indexed direct messages from RAMP (the forum was seized by the FBI in January 2026), and those missives show the RAMP administrator approved Haise’s application, referring to this user as Haise and by their Telegram username: Alexbigboss44.

Searching Intel 471 for Alexbigboss44 reveals this was the Telegram account name shared by the user Rjun on the Russian cybercrime forums Exploit and XSS two years earlier in 2020. The cyber intelligence platform Flashpoint finds Alexbigboss44 is a prolific participant in cybercriminal forums and Telegram channels, primarily focused on the illicit trade of traffic, logs, and corporate access [full disclosure: Flashpoint is an advertiser on this blog].

The Qilin administrator once used the nickname “Rjun” on several forums, and shared their Telegram handle as “Alexbigboss44.” Image: Ke-la.com.

Flashpoint says this user was engaged in high-volume acquisition of Facebook logs and Google Ads accounts to facilitate fraudulent advertising and gambling schemes, and that they functioned as a broker and operator — managing a network of traffickers and purchasing compromised data to fuel their operations.

The link between the Qilin administrator Haise and the much older Rjun and Alexbigboss44 accounts was shared privately earlier this month by IntelHawk, which describes itself as an AI-based platform capable of de-anonymizing threat actors based on historical usernames, stylometry and other signals.

IntelHawk founder and chief technology officer Leo Bogod said an analysis of these identities shows a progression from novice arbitrageur and credit card fraudster in 2018–2019 to a more experienced participant and organizer of complex cybercrime-related activities in 2020–2023, with increasing attention to malware, botnets, and payment infrastructure.

Where does this connection between these threat actor identities lead? Intel 471 finds that by the time Alexbigboss44 was applying for membership to RAMP, Rjun was already a longtime member of several other Russian crime forums, including Darkmarket, Verified, and Zloy. Intel 471 says Rjun signed up at all of these sites with the email address mail-30a@mail.ru.

The identity threat protection firm Spycloud found the email address mail-30a@mail.ru at one time used the password “Rjun132” [Spycloud is also an advertiser on this blog]. A search for that email at the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence shows that it appeared in records maintained by gosuslugi.ru, the official digital platform for state and municipal services in the Russian Federation.

Gosuslugi was breached in late 2025, reportedly exposing more than 20 million records with full names, birth dates, and mobile numbers. According to the leaked Gosuslugi records (via Constella), the address mail-30a@mail.ru belongs to 36-year-old Aleksey Mikhailovich Yakovtsev from St. Petersburg, Russia.

Flashpoint finds Haise has long used a Telegram account with the user ID 118329521, recording more than 5,000 messages from this user since 2018. Records from Russia’s education watchdog Rosobrnadzor reveal that Mr. Yakovtsev went to grade school in Murmansk and that he holds a master’s degree in computing and information systems.

A search on this Telegram ID in Constella shows it is linked to the Russian phone number +79602347275. Pivoting on that phone number in Constella reveals it is connected to the email addresses aleksey1990yakov@mail.ru and rjun123321@mail.ru. IntelHawk finds that +79602347275 belongs to Yakovtsev’s biological sister, and that Aleksey often used his sister’s email address when registering at different websites.

That phone number appears on several airline flight records at Russian travel agencies that have experienced a data breach in recent years, and those records show Aleksey Yakovtsev, born August 18, 1990, flew between St. Petersburg and Murmansk at least three times between 2013 and 2014.

More recent flight records show that while Mr. Yakovtsev has not traveled by plane outside of Russia, he does fly frequently between Saint Petersburg and Sochi. Often called the “Russian Riviera,” Sochi is Russia’s largest resort city, situated along the coast of the Black Sea and about 1,200 miles south of Saint Petersburg by plane.

Attempts to reach Mr. Yakovtsev via email and phone were unsuccessful.

Further reading: GangExposed, an anonymous Twitter/X account that has a history of successfully deanonymizing suspected ransomware actors, reached similar conclusions about Haise’s real-life identity, crediting IntelHawk’s platform for helping to connect the dots.

The Qilin ransomware admin Haise’s now-deleted Telegram account, advertising the affiliate program in July 2024. Image: justpaste.it/iosba.

#9653. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. #9652. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly:  When it comes to English grammar, there are two Big Players that everyone knows of: the Grammarly and ProWritingAid. but you are wondering which one to choose so here we write a detail article which will help you to choose the best one for you so Let's start

What is Grammarly?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.


Features of Grammarly

  • Spelling and Word Suggestion: Grammarly detects basic to advance grammatical errors and also help you why this is an error and suggest to you how you can improve it
  • Create a Personal Dictionary: The Grammarly app allows you to add words to your personal dictionary so that the same mistake isn't highlighted every time you run Grammarly.
  • Different English Style: Check to spell for American, British, Canadian, and Australian English.
  • Plagiarism: This feature helps you detect if a text has been plagiarized by comparing it with over eight billion web pages.
  • Wordiness: This tool will help you check your writing for long and hard-to-read sentences. It also shows you how to shorten sentences so that they are more concise.
  • Passive Voice: The program also notifies users when passive voice is used too frequently in a document.
  • Punctuations: This feature flags all incorrect and missing punctuation.
  • Repetition: The tool provides recommendations for replacing the repeated word.
  • Proposition: Grammarly identifies misplaced and confused prepositions.

  • Plugins: It offers Microsoft Word, Microsoft Outlook, and Google Chrome plugins.


What is ProWritingAid?

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing. 

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Features of ProWriting Aid

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

  • Grammar checker and spell checker: This tool helps you to find all grammatical and spelling errors.
  • Find repeated words:  The tool also allows you to search for repeated words and phrases in your content.
  • Context-sensitive style suggestions:  You can find the exact style of writing you intend and suggest if it flows well in your writing.
  • Check the readability of your content: Pro Writing Aid helps you identify the strengths and weaknesses of your article by pointing out difficult sentences and paragraphs.
  • Sentence Length: It also indicates the length of your sentences.
  • Check Grammatical error: It also checks your work for any grammatical errors or typos, as well.
  • Overused words: As a writer, you might find yourself using the same word repeatedly. ProWritingAid's overused words checker helps you avoid this lazy writing mistake.
  • Consistency: Check your work for inconsistent usage of open and closed quotation marks.
  • Echoes: Check your writing for uniformly repetitive words and phrases.

Difference between Grammarly and Pro-Writing Aid

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

Grammarly vs ProWritingAid

  • Grammarly is a writing enhancement tool that offers suggestions for grammar, vocabulary, and syntax whereas ProWritingAid offers world-class grammar and style checking, as well as advanced reports to help you strengthen your writing.
  • Grammarly provides Android and IOS apps whereas ProWritingAid doesn't have a mobile or IOS app.
  • Grammarly offers important suggestions about mistakes you've made whereas ProWritingAid  shows more suggestions than Grammarly but all recommendations are not accurate
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas the ProWritingAid interface is not friendly as Grammarly.
  • Grammarly is an accurate grammar checker for non-fiction writing whereas ProWritingAid is an accurate grammar checker for fiction writers.
  • Grammarly finds grammar and punctuation mistakes, whereas ProWritingAid identifies run-on sentences and fragments.
  • Grammarly provides 24/7 support via submitting a ticket and sending emails. ProWritingAid’s support team is available via email, though the response time is approximately 48 hours.
  • Grammarly offers many features in its free plan, whereas ProWritingAid offers some basic features in the free plan.
  • Grammarly does not offer much feedback on big picture writing; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.
  • Grammarly is a better option for accuracy, whereas ProWritingAid is better for handling fragmented sentences and dialogue. It can be quite useful for fiction writers.

ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Pricing Difference

  • ProWritingAid comes with three pricing structures. The full-year cost of ProWritingAid is $79, while its lifetime plans cost $339. You also can opt for a monthly plan of $20.
  • Grammarly offers a Premium subscription for $30/month for a monthly plan  $20/month for quarterly and $12/month for an annual subscription.
  • The Business plan costs $12.50 per month for each member of your company.

ProWritingAid vs Grammarly – Pros and Cons

Grammarly Pros

  • It allows you to fix common mistakes like grammar and spelling.
  • Offers most features in the free plan
  • Allows you to edit a document without affecting the formatting.
  • Active and passive voice checker
  • Personal dictionary 
  • Plagiarism checker (paid version)
  • Proofread your writing and correct all punctuation, grammar, and spelling errors.
  • Allows you to make changes to a document without altering its formatting.
  • Helps users improve vocabulary
  • User-friendly interface
  • Browser extensions and MS word add-ons
  • Available on all major devices and platforms
  • Grammarly will also offer suggestions to improve your style.
  • Enhance the readability of your sentence
  • Free mobile apps 
  • Offers  free version

Grammarly Cons

  • Supports only English 
  • Customer support only via email
  • Limits to 150,000 words
  • Subscription plans can be a bit pricey 
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in a premium plan
  • Doesn’t offer a free trial
  • No refund policy
  • The free version is ideal for basic spelling and grammatical mistakes, but it does not correct advanced writing issues.
  • Some features are not available for Mac.

ProwritingAid Pros

  • It offers more than 20 different reports to help you improve your writing.
  • Less expensive than other grammar checkers.
  • This tool helps you strengthen your writing style as it offers big-picture feedback.
  • ProWritingAid has a life plan with no further payments required.
  • Compatible with Google Docs!
  • Prowritingaid works on both Windows and Mac.
  • They offer more integrations than most tools.

ProWritingAid Cons

  • Editing can be a little more time-consuming when you add larger passages of text.
  • ProWritingAid currently offers no mobile app for Android or iOS devices.
  • Plagiarism checker is only available in premium plans.
  • All recommendations are not accurate

Summarizing the Ginger VS Grammarly: My Recommendation

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

  • For example, go for Grammarly  if you are a non-fiction writer
  • Go for ProWritingAid if you are a fiction writer.
  • ProWritingAid is better at catching errors found in long-form content. However, Grammarly is more suited to short blog posts and other similar tasks.
  • ProWritingAid helps you clean up your writing by checking for style, structure, and content while Grammarly focuses on grammar and punctuation.
  • Grammarly has a more friendly UI/UX whereas; ProWritingAid offers complete feedback on big picture writing.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

#9651. XYBench: Helping with the problem behind the question

Truly useful AI assistants need to be able to help users who ask misguided questions—not just users who ask the right question with the right amount of detail. We’re releasing XYBench, a benchmark of 8K+ questions that tests how AI assistants respond to requests based on misconceptions, such as asking how to thicken frosting that keeps sliding off cupcakes when the real problem is that the cupcakes are still too warm to frost. XYBench won the Best Resource Paper Award at EMNLP 2026.

A mismatch between the approach someone asks about and the goal they want to achieve is known as the XY problem: a person wants to accomplish X, assumes a particular approach Y will work, and asks for help with Y. In the cupcake example, the person is so committed to making the frosting stick that they fail to consider the warmth of the cupcake as the true problem to be addressed.

Developed with researchers at Carnegie Mellon, NVIDIA, and Johns Hopkins, XYBench exposes a critical gap in LLMs' ability to troubleshoot problems: recognizing when a user's request is based on an implicit misconception and appropriately redirecting them toward a solution that addresses their actual goal. Drawing on 8,115 real-world questions spanning programming and everyday activities such as cooking and home repair, we introduce a benchmark that measures whether models identify these misconceptions and are able to prioritize effective solutions in their responses.

The models we evaluated on XYBench – Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro – often suggested a solution to the user’s problem but kept their answers focused on the original, mistaken approach. Unlike human reference answers, all five models were less likely to steer users away from that approach and toward a solution suited to their goal.

People use AI systems with different levels of knowledge and may not always know how best to approach a problem. We hope XYBench helps researchers measure whether model improvements make assistants better at recognizing mistaken assumptions, explaining why a proposed approach might not work, and suggesting more effective alternatives—even when users don't know the right questions to ask.

We built XYBench from four sources: 1,557 questions from Stack Overflow, 184 from Stack Exchange, 102 manually curated examples, and 6,272 questions generated from WikiHow guides. For each question, we identified the stated request (Y), what the person explicitly asks for, and the intended request (X)—the underlying goal that can be inferred from context.

For the public forum questions, we used the three highest-scored human answers and the accepted answer, where available, to establish the intended request and possible solutions. We filtered out cases where answering the stated request was judged sufficient. For WikiHow, we used Sonnet 4.5 to generate questions around plausible misconceptions in procedural guides, then refined them to include enough context for an expert to infer the underlying goal without stating it outright. We removed examples where answering the literal request would largely resolve the problem.

A model might spend several paragraphs recommending a more powerful vacuum cleaner, then briefly suggest checking for a clogged hose. If a clog is causing the weak suction, clearing it could solve the problem.

A more helpful answer would recognize that the user wants to restore suction and focus on diagnosing the cause. This draws on pragmatics, the branch of linguistics concerned with how context and communicative intent shape meaning. To test whether models use this understanding in their answers, XYBench measures three aspects of each response:

In XYBench, Claude Sonnet 4.5 serves as the automated judge. It classifies individual suggestions within each model’s response and assesses the answer’s pragmatic emphasis.

To validate Sonnet 4.5’s judgments, two human reviewers independently assessed 500 model responses to XYBench questions. Agreement with the judge, averaged across the reviewers, ranged from 97.5–100% on whether a solution appeared, 84.6–93.3% on misconception identification, and 74.2–79.8% on pragmatic emphasis.

We evaluated Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B, and DeepSeek-V4 Pro on XYBench in a single-turn setting, with one response per question. We evaluated human reference answers separately using the same metrics.

Across all four sources, every model was more likely to include a solution to the stated request (Y) than to the underlying goal (X). On Stack Overflow, stated-request solutions appeared in 75–86% of responses, compared with 59–71% for underlying-goal solutions.

A passing mention of a solution does not make it the focus of an answer. In the vacuum example, a model could briefly suggest unclogging the hose but focus most of its response on buying a more powerful vacuum. We would count that response as containing a solution to the underlying goal, even though the model emphasized the stated request. We measured overall emphasis separately: on Stack Overflow, models focused primarily on the underlying goal in only 35–41% of their responses, and on the stated request in 47–57%. In the remaining responses, models gave similar emphasis to the stated request and the underlying goal.

We also tested whether making the user’s goal explicit would help. In an oracle experiment, we supplied both the stated request (Y) and the intended request (X) alongside each question. On Stack Overflow, Sonnet 4.6’s rate of including a solution to the underlying goal rose from 59% to 67%, but its misconception-identification rate fell from 47% to 34%. Across the sources with human reference answers, every model in this experiment still trailed humans on misconception identification. Supplying intent helped, but did not consistently close the gap with human responses. This suggests that detecting intent is only part of the challenge: models also need to act on it when it diverges from the stated request.

A separate experiment tested whether models could identify useful advice when judging responses instead of writing them. We gave the same five models, plus GPT-4.1, each question with two possible answers: one focused on the literal request and one explaining the misconception and addressing the underlying goal. On Stack Overflow, all six chose the goal-focused answer in 71–84% of cases. By comparison, only 35–41% of the answers written by the five models in our main evaluation primarily focused on the underlying goal. The results expose a gap between recognizing useful advice and producing it, which a multiple-choice test alone would miss.

Researchers can use XYBench to test whether changes to prompting or training help models identify misconceptions, offer solutions to users’ underlying problems, and make those solutions the focus of their answers. Measuring each behavior individually lets researchers see whether progress in one also improves the others.

Future work could test which training methods help models act on inferred intent—AKA what users need and not just what they literally asked for. The XYBench currently covers English-language queries and mainly procedural problems; extending it to other languages, cultures, and conversational settings remains an open direction.

We hope XYBench enables researchers to build models that offer useful advice even when a user’s first question rests on a mistaken assumption.

#9650. Your EC2 Bill is an Architecture Problem, Not an Accounting One

Co-Founder at Munchkins AI - SAAS company building AI agents for healthcare and MSCS Student at Georgia Tech

Co-Founder at Munchkins AI - SAAS company building AI agents for healthcare and MSCS Student at Georgia Tech

Co-Founder at Munchkins AI - SAAS company building AI agents for healthcare and MSCS Student at Georgia Tech

Compute is usually the biggest line on the AWS bill. It’s also the part nobody designs on purpose. Someone picks an x86 On-Demand instance during the first sprint, sizes it “with some headroom,” and that choice quietly sticks around for 2 years.

You can’t fix that from the billing dashboard. Cost is decided much earlier:

The above four things decide compute spend and system resilience. This post walks through each one and ends with a working AWS CDK stack that puts it all together.

AWS names instances like m5.2xlarge, where m is the class, 5 is the generation, and 2xlarge is the size. Class is the part that matters most, because it sets the ratio of vCPU to memory.

If your service is CPU-bound, running it on M instances means paying for memory you never touch. If it’s memory-bound, C instances will force you to over-scale. Profile first, then pick.

EC2 gives you several ways to pay for the same hardware:

Don't run everything On-Demand. Don't run user-facing APIs 100% on Spot either. The pattern that holds up in production is:

A lot of people still think of Spot as an auction where someone outbids you and your instance dies. That isn't how it works anymore. Prices now move slowly based on long-term supply and demand. You can still set a max price (it defaults to the On-Demand price), but most interruptions happen because AWS needs the hardware back for On-Demand or Reserved customers in that AZ, not because the price jumped.

A Spot capacity pool is one instance type in one Availability Zone. c8g.large in us-east-1a is a different pool from c8g.large in us-east-1b, and both are different from c7g.large in us-east-1a.

If your Auto Scaling Group or Spot Fleet only allows one instance type, you're depending on just a few pools. When those get squeezed, your whole tier goes down at once. So list several families and sizes that your service can run on.

When you give AWS a list of pools, the allocation strategy decides which ones it pulls from:

With Spot in the mix, nodes will vanish. Users won’t notice if you handle two things well: draining traffic and storing data.

AWS warns you twice before taking a Spot node back:

Set ECS_ENABLE_SPOT_INSTANCE_DRAINING=true. When the two-minute notice arrives, ECS moves the node’s tasks to healthy nodes. The ALB stops sending new requests to that node and lets the open ones finish.

The catch is that the ALB waits 300 seconds by default, but Spot only gives you 120. If you leave the default, the node dies mid-drain, and users get 502s. Set the deregistration delay and stopTimeout to 60–90 seconds.

Also use awsvpc mode. Each task gets its own IP, so the ALB sends traffic straight to the task.

Anything written to the node’s own disk is lost when the node goes away. You have three choices:

an ECS cluster on a mixed-instance ASG using Graviton families

one On-Demand base node plus an 80/20 Spot/On-Demand split above it, using PRICE_CAPACITY_OPTIMIZED,

an ALB with a deregistration delay that fits inside the Spot window,

an encrypted EFS volume mounted into the tasks.

A couple of things worth calling out. spotInstanceDraining: true is the CDK way to set the agent flag, so you don't have to append it to /etc/ecs/ecs.config yourself. And the nodes run in private subnets, so the ALB is the only thing with a public IP.

Even with the right instances and purchase mix, a few networking line items can take back a big chunk of what you saved.

Cross-AZ traffic and NAT. Data crossing AZs costs $0.01/GB each way. With one NAT Gateway in us-east-1a and nodes spread across three AZs, about two-thirds of your outbound traffic pays that cross-AZ fee on top of the NAT's $0.045/GB processing charge. For real production traffic, run a NAT per AZ. Always add the free gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB so that traffic never touches a NAT.

Public IPv4 addresses. AWS charges $0.005 per hour (about $3.65 a month) for every public IPv4 address, attached or not. Keep cluster nodes in private subnets and clean up unattached Elastic IPs.

The draining mismatch. This one is worth repeating because it's the most common one I see. The ALB's default deregistration delay is 300 seconds. A Spot interruption gives you 120. Leave the default and your users get 502s every time AWS reclaims a node. Set both the deregistration delay and stopTimeout to 60–90 seconds.

None of this is complicated on its own. The savings come from treating these choices as design decisions: right-size the instance family, default to ARM, cover your baseline with a Savings Plan, run peaks on diversified Spot, drain cleanly, and keep state off the host. Do that, and the bill goes down, and the system gets better at handling failure at the same time.

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

With the assembled robot and can in the scene, ask the agent to run the task. Evaluate the simulation behavior using the checks in the next step.

Now that the assets include simulation properties and profile validation, we can now test in an assembled scene and controller. The controller coordinates the UR17G arm’s movement with the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper’s opening and closing. Use the behavior checks below to evaluate the agent-generated task. To understand or adapt the controller yourself, see the Adding a Manipulator Robot tutorial.

Skills used: ‘isaac-sim-remote’, ‘manipulaiton-ik’ and ‘physics-simulation’

The full task tests whether the gripper holds the can during movement and releases it at the target. Reset the scene, then run the approach, grasp, lift, hold, transfer, and release sequence. Compare your run with the opening video and the success criteria below.

Figure 6. The UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper move the beverage can from the yellow pickup marker to the green target in Isaac Sim. Shown at 4× speed.

If your run differs, note where the sequence fails and ask the agent to inspect the scene and generate controls. Reset the can and robot to the same starting state before retrying so you can compare the results.

These results apply to this scripted setup. They do not establish robustness to uncertain object positions, different payloads, or real hardware.

Build your own pick-and-place task with assets from SimReady Central, then use an agent of your choice to help assemble the scene and run it in Isaac Sim.
